title: Kuhusu Matukio ya Zamani / Talking about Past Experiences
bridge: In Swahili, talking about past experiences is similar to English in that you use past tense verbs. However, Swahili has a more straightforward past tense system with fewer irregular verbs compared to English. One key difference is that Swahili does not use auxiliary verbs like 'did' for past tense questions or negatives, and the subject-verb agreement is more consistent. Be cautious not to directly translate English phrases like 'used to' or 'would,' as Swahili expresses habitual past actions differently.
rule: To talk about past experiences in Swahili, use the past tense form of the verb, which typically ends in '-a' for most verbs. For example, 'kuandika' (to write) becomes 'naliandika' (I wrote). Negatives are formed by adding 'ha-' before the verb root, e.g., 'sikuandika' (I did not write). Questions follow the same structure as statements but with a question mark. Habitual past actions are expressed using 'kuwa na' (to be in the habit of) followed by the noun or verb, e.g., 'Niliwa na kufanya' (I used to do).

concept_examples.translation: Yesterday I went to the market.
Last year I had a good trip.
When I was young, I liked to play.
Long ago we used to pick fruits.

common_error.wrong: Jana I did go to the market.
common_error.explanation: English speakers often try to directly translate the auxiliary verb 'did' into Swahili, which is incorrect. Swahili does not use auxiliary verbs for past tense; instead, the verb itself changes to indicate the past.

examples.note: Use 'jana' (yesterday) to frame recent past experiences.

examples.translation: Last week I received a letter.
examples.note: Use 'juma moshi' (last week) for slightly older past events.

examples.translation: Last year I did a lot of work.
examples.note: Use 'mwaka uliopita' (last year) for past events in a specific year.

examples.translation: I received a gift last year.
examples.note: Focus on using the past tense verb 'nilipata' (I received).

examples.translation: Long ago we used to catch fish.
examples.note: Use 'hapo zamani' (long ago) for distant past habits.

examples.original: Nilipokuwa mwanzo, nilikuwa na marafiki wengi.
examples.phonetic: nilipokuwa mwanzo, nilikuwa na marafiki wengi
examples.translation: When I was young, I had many friends.
examples.note: Use 'nilipokuwa mwanzo' (when I was young) for past life stages.

title: Kufanya mipango / Making Plans
bridge: In Swahili, making plans often involves more explicit expressions of agreement and confirmation compared to English. For instance, Swahili speakers frequently use phrases like 'Ndio, tutafanya' (Yes, we will do it) to confirm plans, whereas English speakers might simply say 'Okay' or 'Sure'. Additionally, Swahili tends to use more formal structures when suggesting activities, such as 'Je, tunaweza kufanya...' (Can we do...), which can sound more polite than the direct English equivalent.
rule: To make plans in Swahili, use the structure 'Je, [tunaweza/tunataka] kufanya...' (Can/Do we want to do...) for suggestions, followed by 'Ndio' or 'Hapana' for agreement or disagreement. For confirmation, use 'Tutafanya' (We will do) or 'Sisi tutakuwepo' (We will be there). Remember, Swahili often emphasizes clarity and politeness, so be explicit in your responses.

concept_examples.translation: Can we go on a trip tomorrow?
Yes, we will go on a trip tomorrow.
We will be there at one o'clock.

concept_examples.text: Je, unataka kujikuta kwenye kazi ya jioni?
concept_examples.translation: Do you want to meet at the evening job?
concept_examples.phonetic: /d͡ʒe unataka kujikuta kwɛnye kazi ja joɲi/

common_error.explanation: English speakers often omit the subject 'tunaweza' (we can) and the verb 'kufanya' (to do) when making suggestions in Swahili. Always use the full structure 'Je, tunaweza kufanya...' to ensure clarity and politeness.

examples.translation: Do we want to go to the cinema?
examples.note: Use 'tunataka' (we want) for preferences.

examples.translation: No, I want to go to work.
examples.note: Use 'nataka' (I want) for personal preferences.

examples.translation: Yes, we will be there at two o'clock.
examples.note: Use 'tutakuwepo' (we will be there) for confirmation.

examples.translation: No, we will not be there.
examples.note: Use 'hatutakuwepo' (we will not be there) for disagreement.
Use 'kubadilisha' (to change) for modifications.

examples.translation: Yes, we will change to go in the evening.
examples.note: Use 'tutabadilisha' (we will change) for agreement.

title: Kutoa mashauri / Giving Advice
bridge: In Swahili, giving advice often involves the use of the verb 'kuwa na' (to have) followed by the noun 'mashauri' (advice), which is different from English where we typically use modal verbs like 'should' or 'could'. Swahili also uses the imperative form more frequently than English, which can sound direct but is not rude. Be cautious not to overuse the English structure 'you should' directly, as it doesn't translate well into Swahili.
rule: To give advice in Swahili, you can use the structure 'Ushindwe/Usifie kufanya [action]' (Don't fail/Don't hesitate to do [action]) or 'Ni jambo luku [action]' (It's good to [action]). Another common way is to use the verb 'kuwa na' followed by 'mashauri' and then the action. For example, 'Ni jambo luku kujifunza Kiswahili' (It's good to learn Swahili). Remember, the imperative form is widely accepted and not considered impolite.

concept_examples.translation: Don't fail to work hard.

concept_examples.text: Ni jambo luku kula majani ya kuhifadhi afya.
concept_examples.translation: It's good to eat vegetables to maintain health.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ni d͡ʒambo luku kula mad͡ʒani ja kuhifadhi afja/

concept_examples.translation: Don't fail to hurry.

concept_examples.text: Ni jambo luku kuweka kipande cha kufurahia maisha.
concept_examples.translation: It's good to take time to enjoy life.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ni d͡ʒambo luku kuweka kipande cha kufurahia maisha/

common_error.explanation: The error occurs because learners directly translate 'you should' from English, which sounds unnatural in Swahili. Instead, use phrases like 'Ni jambo luku' or 'Ushindwe kushindwa' to give advice more naturally.

examples.note: Use this structure to encourage action.
This phrase is used to recommend an activity.

examples.translation: Don't hesitate to eat unhealthy food.
examples.note: This structure advises against an action.

examples.original: Ni jambo mbaya kucheka kwa saa nyingi.
examples.phonetic: /ni d͡ʒambo mbaja kʊcheka kwa saa nɪŋɪ/
examples.translation: It's bad to laugh for a long time.
examples.note: Use this to discourage behavior.

examples.translation: Don't fail to prioritize your family.
examples.note: This advises putting something first.

examples.original: Ni jambo luku kuweka afya yako kwanza.
examples.phonetic: /ni d͡ʒambo luku kʊweka afja jako kwanza/
examples.translation: It's good to prioritize your health.
examples.note: Encourages focusing on well-being.

title: Kusema Maoni / Expressing Opinions
bridge: In Swahili, expressing opinions often involves using the verb 'kuona' (to see) or 'kuamini' (to believe) instead of the direct equivalents of 'I think' or 'I believe' in English. Unlike English, where 'I think' is commonly used as a filler, Swahili speakers tend to be more direct and concise. Be cautious not to overuse 'kuona' or 'kuamini' as it may sound repetitive; instead, vary your expressions using phrases like 'kwangu' (in my view) or 'kama unavyoona' (as you see it).
rule: To express opinions in Swahili, use the following structures: 1. 'Ninaamini...' (I believe...) or 'Ninaona...' (I think...) followed by the opinion. 2. For more emphasis, use 'Kwangu...' (In my view...) or 'Kama unavyoona...' (As you see it...). Note that the verb 'kuona' (to see) is often used metaphorically to express opinions, similar to 'I see' in English but with a stronger opinionated tone.

concept_examples.text: Ninaamini kwamba ni jambo la kufurahia.
concept_examples.translation: I believe it is something to be happy about.
concept_examples.phonetic: ninɑʔɑmini kwɑmbɑ ni jɑmbo lɑ kufurɑhia

concept_examples.translation: I think it is a big problem.
In my view, it is something to ensure.

concept_examples.text: Kama unavyoona, ni jambo la kufanya.
concept_examples.translation: As you see it, it is something to do.
concept_examples.phonetic: kɑmɑ unɑvyoʔonɑ ni jɑmbo lɑ kufɑnyɑ

common_error.wrong: I think kwamba ni jambo la kufurahia.
common_error.correct: Ninaamini kwamba ni jambo la kufurahia.
common_error.correct_alt: Ninaona kwamba ni jambo la kufurahia.
common_error.explanation: English speakers often directly translate 'I think' into Swahili, which can sound unnatural. Instead, use 'Ninaamini' or 'Ninaona' to express opinions more fluently. Avoid mixing English structures with Swahili phrases.

examples.original: Ninaamini kwamba ni jambo la kufurahia.
examples.phonetic: ninɑʔɑmini kwɑmbɑ ni jɑmbo lɑ kufurɑhia
examples.translation: I believe it is something to be happy about.
examples.note: Use 'Ninaamini' to express a straightforward opinion.

examples.translation: I think it is a big problem.
examples.note: Use 'Ninaona' to give a thoughtful opinion.

examples.translation: In my view, it is something to ensure.
examples.note: Use 'Kwangu' to emphasize your personal view.

examples.original: Kama unavyoona, ni jambo la kufanya.
examples.phonetic: kɑmɑ unɑvyoʔonɑ ni jɑmbo lɑ kufɑnyɑ
examples.translation: As you see it, it is something to do.
examples.note: Use 'Kama unavyoona' to invite agreement or discussion.

examples.original: Ninaamini kwamba ni jambo la kufikiri tena.
examples.phonetic: ninɑʔɑmini kwɑmbɑ ni jɑmbo lɑ kufikiɾi tɛnɑ
examples.translation: I believe it is something to think about again.
examples.note: Combine 'Ninaamini' with nuanced phrases for deeper opinions.

examples.original: Ninaona kwamba ni jambo la kushirikiana.
examples.phonetic: ninɑʔonɑ kwɑmbɑ ni jɑmbo lɑ kushiriɡiɑnɑ
examples.translation: I think it is something to collaborate on.
examples.note: Use 'Ninaona' with specific contexts for clarity.

title: Kubali na Kutokea / Agreeing and Disagreeing
bridge: In Swahili, agreeing and disagreeing often involve specific phrases and structures that differ from English. For instance, 'Ndiyo' (Yes) and 'Hapana' (No) are straightforward, but expressions like 'Ninafikiri vivyo' (I think so) or 'Sijafikiri vivyo' (I don't think so) are more nuanced. Be cautious with tone, as direct disagreement can be perceived as rude, unlike in English where it's more acceptable.
rule: To agree, use 'Ndiyo' (Yes) or phrases like 'Ninafikiri vivyo' (I think so) or 'Ni kweli' (That's true). To disagree, use 'Hapana' (No) or 'Sijafikiri vivyo' (I don't think so). For softer disagreement, use 'Si kweli' (That's not true) or 'Sijui' (I don't know). Note that Swahili often prefers indirect expressions to avoid confrontation, unlike English where directness is common.

concept_examples.translation: Yes, that's true.
No, I don't think so.
I think so, that's true.
That's not true, I don't know.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often mix 'yes' and 'no' with negative phrases like 'I no think so.' In Swahili, 'Ndiyo' (Yes) should pair with positive phrases, while 'Hapana' (No) pairs with negative ones. Avoid direct translations of English phrases like 'I no think so.'

examples.note: Use 'Ndiyo' for simple agreement, followed by 'ni kweli' for emphasis.
Adds nuance to agreement, showing you're considering the statement.
Direct but polite way to disagree, using 'Hapana' and 'sijafikiri vivyo.'
Stronger disagreement, stating the statement is false.
Avoids direct confrontation by expressing uncertainty.
Indirectly disagrees by questioning the necessity of the statement.

title: Kufanya Kazi za Kila Siku / Describing Daily Routines
bridge: In Swahili, describing daily routines often involves using the present tense with specific time markers, similar to English. However, Swahili uses a more consistent structure with the verb 'kufanya' (to do) and time phrases like 'asubuhi' (morning) or 'jioni' (evening). Unlike English, Swahili does not use auxiliary verbs like 'do' or 'does' for questions, and the word order is more flexible. Be cautious not to directly translate English phrases like 'I am doing' into Swahili, as this can sound unnatural.
rule: To describe daily routines in Swahili, use the present tense of the verb preceded by the subject and followed by a time phrase. For example, 'Asubuhi ninaongea na rafiki yangu' (In the morning, I talk with my friend). Questions are formed by changing the intonation or adding a question word like 'Je, unafanya nini asubuhi?' (What do you do in the morning?). Common time phrases include 'asubuhi' (morning), 'mchana' (afternoon), 'jioni' (evening), and 'usiku' (night).

concept_examples.translation: Every morning I wake up at six.
In the evening I eat food.
At night I take a shower.
In the afternoon I study Swahili.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often directly translate 'I am doing' into Swahili, which sounds unnatural. Instead, use the present tense of the verb with a time phrase, like 'Asubuhi ninafanya kazi' (In the morning, I work).

examples.note: Use 'ninawaoka' to describe waking up in the morning.
Use 'ninafunga' to describe cleaning activities.
Use 'ninajifunza' to describe studying in the afternoon.
Use 'ninaenda' to describe going somewhere.
Use 'ninachukua' to describe taking a shower at night.
Use 'ninaonyesha' to describe watching TV.

title: Kuhusu Afya na Dalili / Talking about Health and Symptoms
bridge: In Swahili, describing health and symptoms often involves more direct and specific vocabulary compared to English. For instance, while English might use phrases like 'I feel sick,' Swahili tends to specify the symptom, such as 'Nina umeme' (I have a headache). Be cautious of false friends like 'kima' (cold) which refers to a cold temperature, not a common cold. Additionally, Swahili often uses verbs to describe symptoms, like 'kuchuka' (to vomit), which is more straightforward than English expressions.
rule: To talk about health and symptoms in Swahili, use the structure 'Nina [symptom]' (I have [symptom]) or 'Sina [symptom]' (I don’t have [symptom]). Common symptoms include 'umeme' (headache), 'mahali' (stomachache), and 'kima' (cold temperature). For verbs, use 'kuchuka' (to vomit) or 'kusirika' (to feel dizzy). Remember to specify the body part if necessary, e.g., 'kina umeme kwenye kichwa' (I have a headache in my head).

concept_examples.translation: I have a headache.
I don’t have a stomachache.
He is vomiting.
I have a cold (temperature).

common_error.wrong: Nina kima kwa ajili ya kushuka.
common_error.explanation: English speakers often incorrectly combine symptoms in a single sentence. In Swahili, it’s clearer to state each symptom separately. 'Nina kima kwa ajili ya kushuka' is awkward; instead, say 'Nina kima na nanchuka' (I have a cold and I’m vomiting).

examples.note: Use 'umeme' for headache, a common physical symptom.
Use 'kusirika' to describe dizziness.
Use 'mahali' for stomachache, a common illness symptom.
Use 'kuchuka' to describe vomiting.
Use 'kima' for cold temperature, not a common cold.
Use 'taabu' for fever and 'sina' to negate.

title: Kutoa na kupeleka msaada / Making Requests and Offers
bridge: In Swahili, making requests and offers often involves more explicit expressions of politeness and respect compared to English. While English uses phrases like 'Can you...' or 'Could you...', Swahili uses specific verbs and structures like 'Tafadhali' (please) and 'Ningekuomba' (I would ask you). Be cautious not to directly translate English phrases, as Swahili often requires a more formal tone. Additionally, Swahili offers often include the word 'kupeleka' (to give) or 'kuotoa' (to offer), which are less common in casual English requests.
rule: To make a request in Swahili, use the structure 'Tafadhali [verb]' for polite requests, or 'Ningekuomba [verb]' for more formal situations. For offers, use 'Nakupa [object]' (I give you) or 'Ninakupa [object]' (I am giving you). Remember to use the correct verb conjugation based on the subject. For example, 'Ninakupa' is 'I am giving you,' while 'Anakupa' is 'He/She is giving you.' Always include 'Tafadhali' for politeness in requests.

concept_examples.translation: Please give me water.
I would ask you to help me.
I give you this book.
I am offering you help.

common_error.explanation: Directly translating English phrases like 'Can you...' often sounds too casual in Swahili. Instead, use 'Tafadhali' or 'Ningekuomba' to maintain politeness and formality. Additionally, ensure the verb 'nipe' (give me) is correctly conjugated to match the subject and object.

examples.note: Use 'Tafadhali' for polite requests and 'nipe' to ask for something.
Combine 'Tafadhali' with the verb 'nionyeshe' (show me) for directions.
Use 'Nakupa' to directly offer something.

examples.translation: I am offering you a hand.
examples.note: Add 'ninakupa' for a more continuous offer of assistance.

examples.translation: I would ask you to help me.
examples.note: Use 'Ningekuomba' for formal requests and 'unisaidie' for asking for help.

examples.translation: I would ask you to bring water.
examples.note: Combine 'Ningekuomba' with 'ulete' (you bring) for formal requests.

title: Kuweza na Kuweza / Expressing Ability and Possibility
bridge: In Swahili, expressing ability and possibility often uses the verb 'kuweza' (to be able to), which is more straightforward than English's 'can' or 'be able to'. Unlike English, Swahili doesn't change 'kuweza' based on the subject, making it simpler but also requiring careful attention to context. Additionally, Swahili uses 'inaweza' for 'he/she/it can', which is a common trap for English speakers who might expect a direct equivalent to 'can'.
rule: To express ability or possibility in Swahili, use the verb 'kuweza' followed by the infinitive of the main verb. For example, 'Ninaweza' (I can), 'Unaweza' (You can), 'Anaweza' (He/She/It can), 'Tunaweza' (We can), 'Mnanaweza' (You all can), 'Wanaweza' (They can). The structure remains consistent regardless of the subject. For possibility, 'inaweza' is often used to indicate that something is possible, similar to 'it is possible' in English.

concept_examples.translation: I can read Swahili.
Can you work today?
Others can reach that place.
It could be true.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often directly translate 'can' into Swahili, which is incorrect. Instead, use 'ninaweza' for 'I can' and follow it with the infinitive of the main verb.

examples.note: Use 'ninaweza' to express personal ability.
Use 'unaweza' to ask about someone else's ability.
Use 'inaweza' to express possibility.
Combine 'inaweza' with 'kuwa' to express uncertainty.
Use 'tunaweza' for group ability.
Use 'wanaweza' for third-person plural ability.

title: Kuhusu Hali ya Hewa / Talking about the Weather
bridge: In Swahili, discussing the weather often involves more descriptive phrases compared to English. For instance, instead of simply saying 'It's sunny,' Swahili speakers might say 'Jua linapoangaza' (The sun is shining). Be cautious of literal translations, as phrases like 'It's raining' in English become 'Ina mvua' (It's raining) in Swahili, but the structure and word order differ. Additionally, Swahili uses specific verbs to describe weather conditions, which may not directly translate to English.
rule: To talk about the weather in Swahili, use the present tense of the verb 'kuwa' (to be) followed by the weather condition. For example, 'Ina jua' (It's sunny) or 'Ina mvua' (It's raining). Adjectives describing the weather often come after the verb. Note that Swahili does not use the subject 'it' as in English; instead, the verb form changes to indicate the subject. For instance, 'Ina baridi' (It's cold) uses 'ina' to show the subject is weather-related.

concept_examples.translation: It's sunny today.
It's raining outside.
It's very cold.
The wind is increasing.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often directly translate 'It is' into Swahili, but Swahili omits the subject 'it' in weather descriptions. Instead, use the verb 'ina' to indicate the weather condition directly. Avoid adding unnecessary subjects or articles.

examples.note: Use 'ina jua' to describe sunny weather. Note the verb 'ina' indicates the subject without needing 'it'.
Simple phrase for rain. Avoid adding 'it is' as in English.
Use 'baridi' for cold weather. Adjectives follow the verb 'ina'.
Use 'inaongezeka' to describe increasing wind. 'Mauaji' is the noun for wind.
Simple phrase for hot weather. 'Joto' means heat or hot.
Use 'samu' to describe dry conditions. Adjective follows 'ina'.
Use 'kuna' for 'there is/are'. 'Mawingu' means clouds, and 'mengi' means many.
'Kalulu' describes light rain. Follows the verb 'ina'.
Use 'inaanza' to describe the beginning of rain. 'Mvua' is the noun for rain.
